title: Its AI agent spent days hacking a company, but sources say OpenAI did not notice for a week
byline: Raphael Satter, Deepa Seetharaman, Kenrick Cai
excerpt: OpenAI noticed after the threat was contained and the FBI was alerted, people familiar with the investigation say.
content_html:
• Summary
  • Companies
  • The agent first tried escaping OpenAI's isolated environment around July 9, two people familiar say
  • Co-founder of victim firm Hugging Face says the intrusion began July 11
  • OpenAI noticed odd behavior from cutting-edge models before hack-sources

WASHINGTON/SAN FRANCISCO, July 24 (Reuters) - The OpenAI agent that broke into tech firm Hugging Face went on a dayslong hacking spree that OpenAI didn't notice until well after the threat was contained and the FBI was alerted, according ​to people familiar with the investigation.

The agent – a program capable of making decisions and executing complex tasks with little or no human oversight – attempted to break out of its isolated testing environment ‌at OpenAI around July 9, according to two of the people.

Sign up here.

The intrusion at Hugging Face, which operates as a repository for AI tools and models, began two days later on July 11 and lasted until July 13, said Thomas Wolf, Hugging Face’s co-founder.

It took several more days for OpenAI to realize its agent was behind the hack, and the two companies only communicated about it for the first time on or around July 20, according to Wolf and three of the people familiar with the investigation.

OpenAI’s public disclosure, on July 21, that one of ​its agents had slipped out of control and carried out the break-in at Hugging Face drew global attention. But many details of the hack, including how long the agent went rogue and OpenAI’s belated knowledge ​of it, are being reported here for the first time.

Hugging Face is preparing a public timeline of the hack, Wolf said, adding that he could not speak to what ⁠happened at OpenAI. In a statement, OpenAI said the hack was unprecedented and “marks an important moment for AI safety.” It added that it was reviewing the incident with outside advisers and would eventually publish a technical report.

A spokeswoman ​said there were "several inaccuracies" in Reuters' reporting but didn't respond when asked to describe them.

The FBI declined to comment about the incident.

The incident, which evoked science fiction scenarios about humans losing control of dangerous AI systems, comes at a delicate ​time for OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. Its executives are preparing for a possible initial public offering that could come as soon as this year to help finance the billions needed to fund its growth in years to come.

OpenAI's loss of control over its AI agent raises new questions about the company’s safety procedures, three cybersecurity experts said.

“Does that mean that they left it unattended and didn’t realize what it was doing? Or maybe they did and didn’t know how to contain it? Both are equally dangerous and alarming,” asked Marley Smith, ​the principal intelligence specialist at the nonprofit World Ethical Data Foundation.

SIGNS OF TROUBLE?

The episode started while OpenAI was testing the cybersecurity prowess of an agent powered by two of OpenAI’s most advanced models, GPT‑5.6 Sol and an unreleased ​model OpenAI has described as “even more capable.” By that point, there were already indications of strange behavior from OpenAI’s technology, according to three sources.

In one case, an agent left notes apparently for future versions of itself, according to three people familiar with the matter. The ‌notes, found in ⁠a part of OpenAI's infrastructure, laid out instructions for how agents could free themselves from OpenAI’s internal constraints, the people said. Earlier tests of the models yielded cases in which monitoring systems had been disconnected, one of the people said.

Reuters could not establish if these incidents were linked to the rogue agent that began escaping on July 9 and attacked Hugging Face on July 11.

Two people familiar with the matter said that it was not until after Thursday, July 16, when Hugging Face

published a blog post, opens new tab

saying it had been hacked by “an autonomous AI agent system,” that OpenAI realized its own agent was responsible. That meant at least a week elapsed between when the model first exhibited signs of ​troubling behavior and OpenAI’s realization that it was responsible for ​the hack.

The weekend of July 18 to 19, ⁠OpenAI staffers spotted clues in internal logs -- records of what OpenAI's systems did -- showing that its agent had escaped from its testing constraints, two of the people familiar with the company's investigation said. Reuters could not establish what prompted OpenAI to sift through the logs.

Four people familiar with OpenAI’s model-training practices say the company often runs several different model ​evaluations at the same time, all of which operate at high speeds and generate such enormous amounts of data that employees sometimes struggle to keep up.

By the time ​OpenAI alerted Hugging Face, the ⁠AI library had already called the FBI to report the hack, according to a person familiar with the matter. Reuters could not establish whether the bureau had opened an investigation.

NEW QUESTIONS ABOUT AUTONOMOUS AGENTS

Autonomous agents are one of the most talked about aspects of the AI industry. Boosters speak of creating armies of virtual employees that work 24 hours a day and send productivity soaring.

But increased autonomy comes with an increased risk of unexpected behavior, and the powerful models they draw on are primed ⁠to take shortcuts ​in order to complete tasks or pass tests.

“The models lie, they cheat, they hack,” said Jeffrey Ladish, whose organization, Palisade Research, studies the ​capabilities and motivations of AI agents.

Ladish said that while the hack of Hugging Face cast an unflattering light on OpenAI, it should spark broader questions over how much all the leading AI companies are willing to invest in onerous security measures while locked in a race with one ​another to deploy the best and fastest models.

“There has to be government oversight,” Ladish said, “because it won’t happen otherwise.”

Reporting by Raphael Satter in Washington and Deepa Seetharaman and Kenrick Cai in San Francisco; Editing by Chris Sanders and Anna Driver

Our Standards: The Thomson Reuters Trust Principles., opens new tab

Reporter covering cybersecurity, surveillance, and disinformation for Reuters. Work has included investigations into state-sponsored espionage, deepfake-driven propaganda, and mercenary hacking.

Deepa is a Reuters technology correspondent covering artificial intelligence and the companies driving its development, including OpenAI and Anthropic. She reports on how advances in AI are reshaping business, politics, and society. This is Deepa's second stint at Reuters. She began her career at the news agency in New York and covered the U.S. auto industry from Detroit before moving to San Francisco to report on Amazon. She was part of a Reuters team named a finalist for the Gerald Loeb Award for Beat Reporting for their coverage of the United Auto Workers. She rejoined Reuters in September 2025. In between, she spent a decade at The Wall Street Journal, where she was the lead reporter covering Facebook and later artificial intelligence following the emergence of ChatGPT. Her reporting included coverage of Instagram's impact on teenage girls and investigations into how AI systems falter in moderating racist and hateful content. She has been part of teams that won the George Polk Award for Business Reporting and the Gerald Loeb Award for Beat Reporting.

Kenrick Cai is a correspondent for Reuters based in San Francisco. He covers Google, its parent company Alphabet and artificial intelligence. Cai joined Reuters in 2024. He previously worked at Forbes magazine, where he was a staff writer covering venture capital and startups. He received a Best in Business award from the Society for Advancing Business Editing and Writing in 2023. He is a graduate of Duke University. Reach him on Signal at @kenrick.01.

blocks.html_en: Deepa is a Reuters technology correspondent covering artificial intelligence and the companies driving its development, including OpenAI and Anthropic. She reports on how advances in AI are reshaping business, politics, and society. This is Deepa's second stint at Reuters. She began her career at the news agency in New York and covered the U.S. auto industry from Detroit before moving to San Francisco to report on Amazon. She was part of a Reuters team named a finalist for the Gerald Loeb Award for Beat Reporting for their coverage of the United Auto Workers. She rejoined Reuters in September 2025. In between, she spent a decade at The Wall Street Journal, where she was the lead reporter covering Facebook and later artificial intelligence following the emergence of ChatGPT. Her reporting included coverage of Instagram's impact on teenage girls and investigations into how AI systems falter in moderating racist and hateful content. She has been part of teams that won the George Polk Award for Business Reporting and the Gerald Loeb Award for Beat Reporting.

content_html_zh:
• 概括
  • 公司
  • 两位知情人士称，该代理在 7 月 9 日左右首次尝试逃离 OpenAI 的隔离环境
  • 受害公司 Hugging Face 联合创始人称入侵始于 7 月 11 日
  • OpenAI 在黑客攻击源之前就注意到了尖端模型的奇怪行为

华盛顿/旧金山，7 月 24 日（路透社）——据知情人士透露，闯入科技公司 Hugging Face 的 OpenAI 特工进行了长达一天的黑客攻击，直到威胁得到遏制并且向 FBI 发出警报后，OpenAI 才注意到这一情况。

据两位知情人士透露，该代理程序是一个能够在很少或根本没有人为监督的情况下做出决策和执行复杂任务的程序，它试图在 7 月 9 日左右突破 OpenAI 的隔离测试环境。

在这里注册。

Hugging Face 联合创始人托马斯·沃尔夫 (Thomas Wolf) 表示，Hugging Face 是人工智能工具和模型的存储库，此次入侵于两天后的 7 月 11 日开始，一直持续到 7 月 13 日。

沃尔夫和三名知情人士表示，OpenAI 又花了几天时间才意识到其代理是此次黑客攻击的幕后黑手，两家公司直到 7 月 20 日左右才首次就此事进行沟通。

OpenAI 于 7 月 21 日公开披露，其一名特工失控闯入 Hugging Face，引起了全球关注。 但这次黑客攻击的许多细节，包括代理失控多久以及 OpenAI 迟来的知识，都是首次在这里报道。

沃尔夫表示，Hugging Face 正在准备公开的黑客攻击时间表，并补充说他无法谈论 OpenAI 发生的事情。 OpenAI 在一份声明中表示，这次黑客攻击是史无前例的，“标志着人工智能安全的一个重要时刻”。 该公司补充说，正在与外部顾问一起审查这一事件，最终将发布一份技术报告。

一位发言人表示，路透社的报道存在“一些不准确之处”，但当被要求描述时没有回应。

联邦调查局拒绝对这一事件发表评论。

这一事件让人想起人类失去对危险人工智能系统的控制的科幻场景，对于 ChatGPT 背后的公司 OpenAI 来说，发生在一个微妙的时刻。 该公司的高管正在为可能的首次公开募股（IPO）做准备，该发行最早可能在今年进行，以帮助为其未来几年的增长提供所需的数十亿美元资金。

三名网络安全专家表示，OpenAI 失去对其人工智能代理的控制引发了有关该公司安全程序的新问题。

“这是否意味着他们让它无人看管并且没有意识到它在做什么？ 或者也许他们知道但不知道如何控制它？ 两者同样危险和令人担忧，”非营利组织世界道德数据基金会的首席情报专家马利史密斯问道。

麻烦的迹象？

这一事件开始时，OpenAI 正在测试一个代理的网络安全能力，该代理由 OpenAI 的两个最先进的模型（GPT-5.6 Sol）和 OpenAI 描述为“能力更强”的未发布模型提供支持。 据三位消息人士称，到那时，OpenAI 的技术已经出现了奇怪行为的迹象。

据三位知情人士透露，在一个案例中，一名特工显然为自己的未来版本留下了笔记。 知情人士称，这些笔记是在 OpenAI 基础设施的一部分中发现的，其中列出了代理如何摆脱 OpenAI 内部限制的说明。 一位知情人士表示，早期对这些模型的测试发现监控系统已被断开。

路透社无法确定这些事件是否与 7 月 9 日开始逃跑并于 7 月 11 日袭击 Hugging Face 的流氓特工有关。

两名知情人士称，直到7月16日星期四之后，《抱脸》

published a blog post, opens new tab

OpenAI 表示，它被“一个自主人工智能代理系统”黑客攻击，并意识到是自己的代理负责。 这意味着从该模型首次表现出令人不安的行为迹象到 OpenAI 意识到它对此次黑客攻击负责，至少已经过去了一周的时间。

两位熟悉该公司调查的人士表示，7 月 18 日至 19 日的周末，OpenAI 工作人员在内部日志（OpenAI 系统所做的记录）中发现了线索，显示其代理已经逃脱了测试限制。 路透社无法确定是什么促使 OpenAI 筛选日志。

四位熟悉 OpenAI 模型训练实践的人士表示，该公司经常同时运行多个不同的模型评估，所有这些模型都高速运行并生成大量数据，以至于员工有时难以跟上。

据一位知情人士透露，当 OpenAI 向 Hugging Face 发出警报时，该 AI 库已经致电 FBI 报告此次黑客攻击事件。 路透社无法确定该局是否已展开调查。

关于自治代理的新问题

自主代理是人工智能行业最受关注的方面之一。 支持者谈到创建虚拟员工大军，每天 24 小时工作并大幅提高生产力。

但自主权的增加伴随着意外行为风险的增加，而他们所利用的强大模型已经准备好走捷径以完成任务或通过测试。

“模型撒谎、作弊、黑客攻击，”杰弗里·拉迪什 (Jeffrey Ladish) 说，他的组织 Palisade Research 研究人工智能代理的能力和动机。

Ladish 表示，虽然 Hugging Face 的黑客攻击给 OpenAI 带来了不讨人喜欢的影响，但它应该引发更广泛的问题：有多少领先的人工智能公司愿意在繁重的安全措施上投资，同时陷入一场部署最佳和最快模型的竞赛。

拉迪什说：“必须有政府监督，否则这种情况就不会发生。”

为路透社报道网络安全、监控和虚假信息的记者。 工作包括调查国家支持的间谍活动、深度造假驱动的宣传和雇佣兵黑客行为。

Deepa 是路透社技术记者，报道人工智能和推动其发展的公司，包括 OpenAI 和 Anthropic。 她报道了人工智能的进步如何重塑商业、政治和社会。 这是迪帕第二次在路透社任职。 她在纽约的新闻机构开始了自己的职业生涯，在底特律报道美国汽车行业，然后搬到旧金山报道亚马逊。 她是路透社团队的一员，因其对美国汽车工人联合会的报道而入围杰拉尔德·勒布节拍报道奖决赛。 她于 2025 年 9 月重新加入路透社。 在此期间，她在《华尔街日报》工作了十年，担任首席记者，报道 Facebook 以及 ChatGPT 出现后的人工智能报道。 她的报道包括 Instagram 对少女的影响的报道，以及对人工智能系统在调节种族主义和仇恨内容方面如何犹豫不决的调查。 她所在的团队曾荣获商业报道乔治波尔克奖和节拍报道杰拉尔德勒布奖。

Kenrick Cai 是路透社驻旧金山记者。 他负责谷歌、其母公司 Alphabet 和人工智能领域的研究。 蔡于 2024 年加入路透社。 他此前曾在《福布斯》杂志工作，担任报道风险投资和初创企业的特约撰稿人。 2023 年，他获得了商业编辑与写作促进协会颁发的最佳商业奖。 他毕业于杜克大学。 通过 Signal 联系他：@kenrick.01。
